clue.text: They appear unswingable however large the room

definitions.text: They appear unswingable however large the room

parts.words: They appear unswingable however large the room
parts.note: the saying 'no room to swing a cat' is turned round: these cats have no tail to swing them by

explanation.surface: Some objects that cannot be swung even in a spacious hall.
explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom 'not enough room to swing a cat' means a cramped space; a cat from the Isle of Man is born tailless, so no room is big enough.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man breed is famously tailless, so there is nothing to grip and swing.

clue.text: Sound speed ratio an elevation for shooting

parts.note: the Mach number is the ratio of a speed to the speed of sound

explanation.surface: Measuring how fast a sound travels, and a raised spot for firing.
explanation.walkthrough: A machan is a raised platform in a tree used in India for hunting tigers.
explanation.definitionFit: A machan is a tree platform from which hunters in India shoot game.

clue.text: No NCO, Monsieur? On the contrary

definitions.text: No NCO, Monsieur? On the contrary

indicators.note: contradicting the 'No', the run of letters across the opening words does spell out a sergeant-type rank, read straight through

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is told he is not a sergeant, and replies that he is.
explanation.walkthrough: The French 'Monsieur' makes 'No' look like 'Non'; 'On the contrary' says the opening letters, run together without the gaps, are exactly an NCO after all.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for non-commissioned officer, such as a corporal or sergeant.

clue.text: A man of donnish invention

parts.note: the 'Don' invented is Don Quixote, so the man is the Spanish author who created him

explanation.surface: A scholar who comes up with academic schemes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'donnish' looks like 'academic' (a don is a university teacher) but points to Don Quixote, the invention of the Spanish novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish writer created the knight Don Quixote, a character of his own devising.

clue.text: Street in which old lady starts sewing-bee ?

definitions.text: Street in which old lady starts sewing-bee ?

parts.words: Street in which old lady starts sewing-bee ?
parts.note: the Old Lady is the Bank of England, on a City of London street whose name is also what you do to begin sewing

explanation.surface: A road where an elderly woman launches a sewing circle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bank of England is nicknamed 'the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street'; to start sewing you pass the cotton through the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The London street housing the Bank of England is named for the first step of stitching.

clue.text: The whitewashed wall, the nicely — floor" (Goldsmith)

definitions.text: The whitewashed wall, the nicely — floor" (Goldsmith)

parts.words: The whitewashed wall, the nicely — floor" (Goldsmith)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Oliver Goldsmith's poem The Deserted Village, describing the village inn's interior

explanation.surface: A line of verse about a tidy country inn, with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Goldsmith's The Deserted Village (1770): floors were strewn with sand and swept, a mark of a well-kept room.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing participle describes a floor smoothed or strewn with grit, completing Goldsmith's line.

clue.text: All, down, out this grassland went a grey mare

definitions.text: All, down, out this grassland went a grey mare

parts.words: All, down, out this grassland went a grey mare
parts.note: the Devon folk song Widecombe Fair has Tom Pearce's grey mare go 'all ___, down ___, out ___ lee', the same word after each

explanation.surface: A grey mare wandered everywhere across the meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: Widecombe Fair is an English folk song: Tom Pearce's grey mare carries riders 'all along, down along, out along lee', lee being grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: The word fills each gap in the song's refrain, meaning onward or forward.

clue.text: Peacefully fitting end ?

parts.note: the bird of peace has a rear end, and a woodworking joint shaped like that fans out to fit snugly

explanation.surface: A calm, appropriate conclusion to a life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fitting end' suggests a suitable death; instead the end is a bird's rear, and the joint named after it fits pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedge-shaped woodworking joint is named for the fanned rear of the bird symbolising peace.

clue.text: Teaching a horse to come into line ?

definitions.text: Teaching a horse to come into line ?

parts.words: Teaching a horse to come into line ?
parts.note: to dress is the military term for forming ranks in line, and this equestrian art is training a horse in precise movements

explanation.surface: Bringing a horse to order.
explanation.walkthrough: In drill, soldiers 'dress' when they straighten their line; the equestrian discipline takes its name from the French for training.
explanation.definitionFit: The equestrian art of training a horse in precise, controlled movements.

clue.text: Quite like a nursery gardener

parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite ___, how does your garden grow?' supplies the word after 'quite'

explanation.surface: Praise for someone who rather resembles a children's-garden worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nursery' points to a nursery rhyme, not a plant nursery: Mary of the rhyme is a gardener, and she is 'quite' this.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the gardening Mary is described as perverse and awkward, the word that follows 'quite'.

clue.text: Blimey-Eve's switched to Labour !

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like blimey

indicators.note: the letters of the name are switched around into a new order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise that Eve has defected to the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switched' rearranges the name into its other spelling. 'Labour' looks like the British political party but means unpaid work owed to a feudal lord; 'Blimey' is a British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A corvée was compulsory unpaid work demanded by a lord or state, a form of forced toil.

clue.text: Experienced by Alice when she hit her head on the roof

definitions.text: Experienced by Alice when she hit her head on the roof

parts.words: Experienced by Alice when she hit her head on the roof
parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's story Alice grows so tall that her head presses against the ceiling, literal aches from getting bigger

explanation.surface: Alice's bump on the head in Wonderland.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means aches felt by children as they grow, or early troubles of a venture; Alice's growth literally hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Aches blamed on a child's rapid growth, here taken literally for Alice's sudden enlargement.

clue.text: Scent from a foreign city

parts.note: Roma is the Italian name for Rome, so the city as foreigners call it

explanation.surface: A fragrance imported from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foreign city' means a city named in its own language: Rome is ROMA in Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: A scent and a pleasant smell or fragrance are the same thing.

clue.text: Does away with a lesser brother at the portals

parts.note: bro is a shortened, lesser form of the word brother
portals are entrances, gates

explanation.surface: A younger sibling standing at the doors is sent packing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lesser brother' suggests a younger sibling but means the word cut down to BRO; 'at the' only links it to GATES.
explanation.definitionFit: To abrogate a law or agreement is to repeal or abolish it.

clue.text: Bats building belfries ?

parts.note: read as cricket, it is batting very defensively; read literally, it is masonry work of the kind that builds bell towers, where bats roost

explanation.surface: Bats constructing their own bell towers.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who blocks every ball without trying to score is said to do this; literally it is laying stones into walls, as for a belfry.
explanation.definitionFit: Obstructive, purely defensive batting in cricket is named after building with masonry.

clue.text: Lordly. South Down byway winding about

indicators.note: the lane goes round the outside of the other pieces

parts.note: a lane is a narrow winding byway
taken as written

explanation.surface: An aristocrat wanders a lane on the South Downs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' sets the lane around the other pieces. Lansdowne is the title of a British marquess, hence 'Lordly'; the South Downs are chalk hills in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is a British peerage title, the Marquess of Lansdowne, so it belongs to nobility.

clue.text: Naval craft shortly to join up and disappear as it would

parts.note: sub is the short form of submarine, a naval craft
to merge is to join up

explanation.surface: A warship briefly links up with others, then vanishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as it would' refers back to the submarine: to go under water is what a sub does.
explanation.definitionFit: To go under the surface and vanish is what a submarine does when it dives.

clue.text: Why Adam and Eve could not have been champing to be at the pictures ?

definitions.text: Why Adam and Eve could not have been champing to be at the pictures ?

parts.words: Why Adam and Eve could not have been champing to be at the pictures ?
parts.note: the toothless have nothing to champ with; Adam and Eve's garden placed at a London gallery spells out the word

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about why the first couple were not eager to see a film.
explanation.walkthrough: Their garden (EDEN) goes beside the Tate gallery ('the pictures') to make the word for toothless animals, who cannot champ (chew).
explanation.definitionFit: Toothless mammals such as sloths and anteaters belong to this group and cannot chew.

clue.text: Don't see the clue ? Then you've got the word

definitions.text: Don't see the clue ? Then you've got the word

parts.words: Don't see the clue ? Then you've got the word
parts.note: if you fail to spot the point, the word describing you is the answer, so failing to see it gives it

explanation.surface: A taunt to a stuck solver: if you're baffled, you've already solved it.
explanation.walkthrough: The paradox is the point: a solver who cannot see the clue's meaning is lacking in insight, which is exactly what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lacking judgment or perception fails to notice or understand things.

clue.text: The Adjutant-General a weakling-I think so too

parts.note: AG is the abbreviation for Adjutant-General
a reed is something weak, as in a broken reed

explanation.surface: A senior officer calls someone a feeble specimen, and the speaker concurs.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'broken reed' is a weak, unreliable person; 'a' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying you concur with someone is the same as saying you think so too.

clue.text: Tried to catch a rhombus, like ?

definitions.meaning: a rhombus has corners, so it is a shape with corners

explanation.surface: Someone attempted to catch a diamond-shaped object.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is fishing; the second describes a shape having corners, like a rhombus.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishing with a hook, and having corners like a rhombus, share the same past-tense word.

clue.text: Herb, the beak's swallowed crude rubber-get a drink

parts.note: mint is a herb

indicators.note: the magistrate's letters take the rubber inside them as if gulping it down

parts.note: beak is British slang for a magistrate, a JP or Justice of the Peace; the 's stands for has
ule is a Central American tree yielding a crude rubber

explanation.surface: A magistrate gulps down a mouthful of raw rubber, then reaches for a cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beak' is British slang for a magistrate; 'swallowed' tucks the rubber inside the magistrate's initials. 'get' only links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a cocktail of bourbon, sugar, and crushed mint served over ice, associated with Kentucky.

clue.text: For jet-set crossword addicts?

parts.note: a large airliner bears this name, and so does an extra-large crossword for keen solvers

explanation.surface: Puzzles for wealthy travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: A big airliner (the Boeing 747) and an outsize puzzle share the same word for something huge.
explanation.definitionFit: The word for something huge names both a big jet airliner and an oversized crossword.

clue.text: No run-about reverses : god, that's fishy !

indicators.note: the indicator turns the whole two-word run back to front

parts.note: taken as written
to gad is to run about idly

explanation.surface: A refusal to let anyone gad about is turned round; something about this deity smells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverses' turns NO + GAD into DAGON. 'fishy' is the definition's sting: Dagon, god of the Philistines, was pictured as half fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Dagon was a Philistine deity traditionally depicted with a fish's tail.

clue.text: Prepares to go back to battle -or back to writing

definitions.text: Prepares to go back to battle

parts.note: the rear is the back
MS is short for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: Getting ready for another war, or returning to one's pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' and 'to' are links: the second half builds REAR (back) beside MS (manuscript).
explanation.definitionFit: A nation that rearms supplies itself with weapons again, readying for war.

clue.text: A firework may be strikingly revolutionary for a time

definitions.meaning: a spinning firework fixed by a pin, also called a Catherine wheel
in a striking clock a wheel set with pins turns to lift the hammer, so it revolves to strike the hour

explanation.surface: A rocket that might cause a brief political upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' links the two senses. 'revolutionary' means turning round, not rebellious; 'strikingly' refers to a clock striking, and 'for a time' to telling the hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a spinning Catherine wheel firework and a pin-set wheel in a clock's striking train carry this name.

clue.text: Previously letters were no different

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are made different, rearranged

explanation.surface: In the past, the letters arriving were just the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters' tells you to work on the letters of WERE NO; 'different' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic phrase meaning before this time, formerly.

clue.text: Rose to dance with Des for a change

indicators.note: the letters are altered, changed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone named Rose takes to the floor with Des as a change of partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a woman's name but is the past tense of rise; 'for a change' shuffles DANCE and DES.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise and to climb upward are the same motion, both in the past tense here.
